statement: A valve-controlled two-stage brew (percolation then immersion) lets you develop acidity/florals and sweetness/body on separate clocks.
mechanism: Percolation with the valve open extracts the fast-dissolving acids and aromatics with fresh, moving water (clarity + brightness). Closing the valve switches to immersion, where extraction is driven by contact time — reaching the mid-curve sugars for sweetness and body without more turbulence. Splitting the brew decouples two goals that a single continuous pour forces you to trade off.
appliesWhen: coffees where you want both high clarity AND developed sweetness
strategyImplication: When the radar asks for clarity AND sweetness together (usually a conflict), reach for a staged percolation→immersion method instead of compromising in the middle.

statement: Outflow resistance (holding water in immersion) builds sweetness and body through contact time, not agitation.
mechanism: Closing the valve stops percolation and lets the slurry steep. Extraction continues via time and diffusion rather than turbulence, so you reach the mid-curve sugars (sweetness) and pull more dissolved solids (body) without the fines migration that agitation causes — avoiding astringency. Time is the gentle sweetness lever.
appliesWhen: delicate/aromatic coffees where agitation risks astringency
strategyImplication: To add sweetness/body while protecting a fragile cup, extend contact time instead of pouring harder or grinding much finer.

statement: With an immersion stage carrying the extraction, you can grind coarser on a dense, aromatic coffee to protect clarity and florals.
mechanism: Coarse grind (~700µm here) lowers percolation resistance and produces fewer fines, which is where astringency and muddiness come from in fragile high-value coffees. Extraction that a finer grind would normally supply is instead provided by the immersion stage's contact time. You get enough extraction without the fines penalty — clarity and aromatics survive.
appliesWhen: dense anaerobic naturals / Geisha / delicate florals
strategyImplication: Pair a coarser grind with an immersion/hold when clarity+florals are the priority on a premium coffee; let time, not fineness, do the extracting.

statement: Low-TDS, balanced Mg/Ca water (~50 ppm) gives enough extraction power for clarity and vibrant acidity without the harshness higher mineral/alkalinity adds.
mechanism: Magnesium and calcium are the ions that actively pull flavour; a modest, balanced ~50 ppm gives real extraction power while keeping total dissolved content low, so acids stay bright and the cup stays transparent. Higher GH/alkalinity would raise extraction but buffer acidity and risk a heavier, duller, harsher cup.
strategyImplication: For clarity + vibrant acidity, spec low-TDS balanced-mineral water; don't reach for high-hardness or high-buffer water.

statement: Moderate brew temperature (~92°C) on a fragile anaerobic natural preserves volatile florals while still extracting sugars.
mechanism: Volatile aromatic compounds (hibiscus, red florals) are heat-sensitive; near-boiling water can blow past them and pull harsher solubles from an already-intense ferment. ~92°C is hot enough to extract a light roast's sugars but cool enough to keep the delicate top notes intact and the cup clean rather than boozy.
strategyImplication: Protect aromatics on fragile ferments with a moderate temp; reserve hotter water for dense, under-developed light roasts that need the energy.

statement: Cooler water + a coarser grind + minimal agitation biases a brew toward sweetness and balance, suppressing bitterness.
mechanism: Lower temperature limits extraction of the late, bitter/phenolic compounds; a coarser grind keeps flow efficient so the cup isn't under-extracted despite the cooler water; few, gentle pours reduce fines migration and astringency. Together they land mid-curve — sweet and rounded — rather than pushing extraction into harshness.
appliesWhen: washed/medium coffees where sweetness+approachability is the goal
not ideal for dense, very light roasts (risk under-extraction)
strategyImplication: When the goal is sweetness/balance over intensity, drop temp (~90–92°C), coarsen grind, and minimise agitation.

statement: Brew ratio trades concentration for clarity: tighter (~1:15) builds sweetness and body; wider (~1:17) increases flavour separation.
mechanism: A tighter ratio raises beverage TDS (strength), so sweetness and body read louder. A wider ratio dilutes the cup, spreading the same solubles thinner so subtle, distinct notes become individually perceptible — clarity and separation at the cost of intensity.
appliesWhen: iced coffee: concentrate the pour to pre-offset planned ice dilution
strategyImplication: Pick ratio by intent: ~1:15 when Sweetness/Body lead; ~1:17 when Clarity/separation leads. For iced, concentrate further (~1:10-11) to survive dilution.

statement: A large bloom (3–4× the dose) degasses fresh/light roasts thoroughly, giving a more uniform extraction bed.
mechanism: CO₂ trapped in fresh, lightly-roasted coffee repels water and causes uneven extraction. A generous bloom (3–4× dose) saturates fully and releases that gas before the main pours, so subsequent water contacts the grounds evenly — raising extraction uniformity and sweetness.
strategyImplication: For fresh/light coffees, bloom at 3–4× dose (not the usual 2×) to degas before extracting.
